Democrat Kreiss-Tomkins says his successful gubernatorial campaign 'covered every corner' of Alaska
articles.description: Democrat Kreiss-Tomkins says his successful gubernatorial campaign 'covered every corner' of Alaska AP News Democrat wins Alaska governor’s seat for first time in nearly 30 years The Guardian Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins wins race for Alaska governor, replaces a Republican NPR JKT wins governor’s race, flipping seat blue in Dunleavy referendum Alaska's News Source JKT declares victory after topping 50% in Alaska
articles.content: JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins said Saturday that being the first Democrat elected governor in Alaska in nearly 30 years holds special meaning for him and he credits his win to an ambitious campaign that “covered every corner of the state.” Winning as a Democrat on a statewide level in Alaska can be like “working against gravity,” he said in an interview with The Associated Press. The 37-year-old former state representative, who often goes by JKT, also said he was proud of the “big-tent base of support” he received from Alaskans of all political backgrounds. Kreiss-Tomkins traveled more than 40,000 miles (64,000 kilometers) within the vast state to pitch himself to voters, including hundreds of miles (kilometers) by snow machine and by boat to visit rural villages, according to his campaign. Most communities in Alaska are not connected to the main road system and often are only accessible by air or water. The campaign said it had more than 10,000 individual donors. Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republicans in the Nov. 3 general election, including Bernadette Wilson. Wilson was endorsed by President Donald Trump, who carried the state in each of his presidential races. Trump announced the endorsement while in Alaska last month for a rally in support of GOP candidates including U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan. Messages seeking comment were left with Wilson’s campaign Friday and Saturday. The two other Republicans in the race — Dave Bronson, a former mayor of Anchorage, and Treg Taylor, a former state attorney general — wished Kreiss-Tomkins success. His victory means Democrats will control governor’s offices in 30 states, including several they flipped after years of Republican control. Kreiss-Tomkins succeeds Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy, who was barred by term limits from seeking a third consecutive stint in office. Kreiss-Tomkins said he ran into Dunleavy on Saturday at a state office building in Anchorage, and the two spoke in Dunleavy’s office. “I appreciated the conversation. It was gracious. He’s been very open and wanting to be helpful,” Kreiss-Tomkins said. Kreiss-Tomkins said during the campaign that over the last eight years, Alaska became “broken” and experienced a “loss of optimism.” He emphasized a willingness to compromise and work across party lines and said he wanted a Cabinet with Republicans, Democrats and independents. He focused on issues including affordability and advocated for full funding of K-12 public schools. Republican U.S. Sen. Lisa Murkowski was among those who endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins, as did former governors including her father, Republican Frank Murkowski; Bill Walker, an independent; and Tony Knowles, the state’s last Democratic governor, who left office in 2002 after two terms. Kreiss-Tomkins said he is still working on assembling his team. He will be sworn in Dec. 7 along with his lieutenant governor, Zac Johnson, an independent. Kreiss-Tomkins said his decade-long experience in the Legislature will be an asset in his new role. One of the first issues he hopes to tackle during the legislative session beginning in January is passage of an education budget that he wants to see happen quickly. Legislative leaders have outlined plans to organize bipartisan coalitions in both the House and Senate.

Just believe: Much improved Romeo not willing to concede against anybody
articles.content: Never in her two decades of coaching high school volleyball has Stacy Williams seen one of her teams improve as much over three months than this year’s team at Romeo. The Bulldogs have gone through a season where they struggled to gain wins back in August to a side that has reached No. 9 in the MIVCA Division 1 rankings, finish second in a deep Macomb Area Conference Red Division, win district and regional titles even though they weren’t predicted to do so at the start of the postseason and navigate their way to Tuesday’s Division 1 state quarterfinals at St. Clair Community College’s SC4 Fieldhouse. Romeo’s opponent is longtime state powerhouse Birmingham Marian, which has won five state titles with multiple state runner-up showings and Final Four berths, especially since the early 2000s. “We have nine seniors on this team, but only three really played significant minutes last season. We lost a good group last year when we went all the way to the regional finals,” said Williams. “We had some girls that were playing a little bit out of position from where we were used to playing in the school or club last year and it took some time. But I honestly think this team has improved more since the beginning of the season to now probably more than any other team I’ve coached. They have come a long ways and they are really playing well right now. “Marian is really good and they always are one of the best teams in the state. We know that,” added Williams. “But we made some changes (last month) to the way we play defense and the way we attack (the net). We are a much better team right now than we were just about a month ago.” Marian (42-5-0) defeated Romeo at some tournaments early in the campaign and are currently ranked second in the state in the D-1 rankings. The Mustangs upset top-ranked Farmington Hills Mercy in the regional finals last Thursday. Romeo is led by a host of talented players who shine at both the club and high school levels and collectively they have played through a tough schedule. The Bulldogs lost to rival Utica Eisenhower three times – all sweeps – during the regular season before upsetting the Eagles in a late-season tournament and again in the district semifinals in a five-set classic back on Nov. 4. “We believe right now that we can play with everybody,” said Williams. “That may have not been the case earlier in the season. But we grew as a team, made some changes, and we started beating some teams. I think when we beat Eisenhower in districts and they were ranked (sixth), I think they really started to believe.” Eleanor Williams, a powerful left-handed outside and right-side hitter who is capable of playing all-around, is the coach’s daughter who has been on varsity all four years and helped the Bulldogs reached the regional finals last season. Seniors Christina Rosenow (MB/S) and Layla Babich have also been around for 100s of games. There are six other seniors on the roster hungry to advance to the final weekend of the season. “This senior group has really stepped up,” smiled Williams. “They have led us and we just keep getting better. “It’s exiting to have my daughter here, too, for four years. But sad to because it’s going to end soon. This is the final week of the season and it’s sad that it’s coming to an end,” added Williams. “Being able to coach your own daughter in high school is special. She’s had a great career for Romeo and been one of our leaders for a while now.” Eleanor Williams is being courted by some NCAA Division I and Division II schools, not to mention some smaller colleges as well. She wants to go into pre-med. “I think Eleanor ahs the right (mindset) and head on her shoulders and has gone through this (process) even though I know that can be difficult trying to find the right match both for academics and wanting to play college volleyball,” added Coach Williams. “I’ve coaches a few girls that have gone onto play in college and I know it’s a process. But there isn’t a doubt that Eleanor and some of the other girls can play at that level. We have some talented girls on this team.” As for now, the girls volleyball season will come to a close this week with the state quarterfinals on Tuesday, state semifinals on Thursday and Friday in Battle Creek and all four state finals matches this Saturday at Battle Creek’s Kellogg Arena. “We know this is the last week. We also know that we always go out there and play hard and believe that we have a chance to win,” added Williams. “I think when you have a large group of seniors who understand that the tournament is the end, they always go out there and play hard and hope for the best. You have to have the right (mental approach).”

A Mayan ceremony in Guatemala honors Nobel winner Miguel Ángel Asturias as his ashes return home
articles.content: GUATEMALA CITY, Guatemala (AP) — A Mayan ceremony held Saturday at an archaeological site in Guatemala’s capital paid tribute to Nobel Prize-winning author Miguel Ángel Asturias, whose ashes returned to his Central American country this week after decades abroad. The ritual at the Kaminal Juyú site brought together the writer’s family and special guests, including Nobel Peace Prize laureate Rigoberta Menchú Tum. The altar was adorned for the ceremony with white, purple, red and yellow flowers, representing the four cardinal directions. There were also candles, incense and cinnamon. Menchú approached the 32-kilogram (70-pound) green jade urn that holds Asturias’ ashes before the ritual, placing her hands upon it. She then offered a prayer, spoke to the urn and kissed it. “Today, we are here, honored by the eternal presence of Don Miguel Ángel Asturias, not only in Guatemala, but throughout the world,” she said. She later encouraged the Guatemalan people to keep the writer’s memory alive by reading his works. The remains of Asturias arrived in Guatemala on Thursday from France, where the writer had been buried following his death in exile in 1974. Asturias died of cancer in Madrid seven years after receiving the Nobel Prize in Literature. His work is considered a precursor to Magical Realism and a key factor in the boom of Latin American literature during the 1960s and 1970s. He went into exile after a 1954 coup led by Gen. Carlos Castillo Armas, who revoked his passport and stripped him of his Guatemalan citizenship, labeling him a communist. Asturias’ final visit to Guatemala took place in 1966. By then, the country was already gripped by violence and repression, fueled by a war between the army and guerrilla forces. He took part in social protests and supported the recognition of the rights of Indigenous peoples. But he also faced accusations of racism over the contents of his college thesis. On Saturday, ancestral knowledge guide Tat Juan José Chirizcuat, who led the ritual, explained that the ceremony presented an opportunity to seek forgiveness and foster reconciliation in light of the different views that people have of the author. The author’s son also made a call for unity. “My father has arrived in Guatemala; may his arrival serve to unite Guatemala,” Miguel Ángel Asturias Amado said. The ashes will lie in state at the National Palace of Culture, allowing the public to pay tribute to the writer through Saturday. On Sunday, they will be interred at a monument within the Miguel Ángel Asturias Cultural Center.

articles.title: SpaceX returned its Starship rocket on Saturday—but there's a catch
articles.description: It felt like stepping into the future.
articles.content: STARBASE, Texas—The black and silver ship fell out of the sky, emerging from the cloud deck near the very end of its flight. Incongruously, the rocket flew horizontal until the last moment when three Raptor rocket engines ignited and it swooped into a vertical position. Slowly, gently, haltingly, the Starship upper stage eased its way toward the waiting tower where two arms extended outward, awaiting expectantly. The margins are so incredibly narrow. Two nubs on either side of the rocket, each protruding only about one foot, were the only purchase the rocket would have on the arms. Then, less than a minute after it came into view, the Starship upper stage was snagged by the launch tower, as snug as you like. And so it was all over. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, had just taken a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Where was Nvidia’s security team?
articles.description: Nvidia’s security chief quietly left in August, and now that CEO Jensen Huang has stepped down over his relationships, including one with an executive at a company suspected of funneling chips to China, a former intelligence officer says it’s the kind of leak that runs everyday conversations, which most corporate security teams are poorly equipped to catch.
articles.content: Outsiders had little reason to notice when Nvidia’s longtime chief security officer and head of product security stepped down in August. Just two and a half months later, CEO Jensen Huang himself left the company over growing questions about his extramarital relationships — starting with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company that U.S. investigators suspect of funneling Nvidia chips to China, then widening to reports about two separate affairs with Nvidia employees. At the time, David Reber, who spent four years as CSO and seven at Nvidia overall, said he was leaving for health reasons. “This wasn’t a pivot I had planned. But I know what needs to come first: family and health,” he wrote on LinkedIn in late August, disclosing that he’d been diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson’s more than two years ago. Reber’s replacement, Saša Zdjelar, previously spent 17 years at ExxonMobil in Houston, leaving as a senior IT manager before spending one year at Salesforce and several years at the cybersecurity company ReversingLabs. Zdjelar didn’t respond to questions Thursday about the transition or what the security team knew. Nothing public connects Reber’s or Zdjelar’s role changes to the Megaspeed matter, but it seems fair to wonder what Nvidia’s security team knew about the government’s scrutiny of Megaspeed and about Huang’s relationships, and whether anyone raised concerns. Reber didn’t respond to questions Thursday. Nvidia also has not answered our related questions. Relationships between a CEO and his employees typically fall to HR, legal and the board, not security. But security specialists say any affair — even one inside the office — can give a foreign intelligence service leverage over an exec who wants it kept quiet. And Huang’s relationship with an executive at Megaspeed, a company under federal investigation, wasn’t an office matter at all. (Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.) Still, spotting the clues isn’t easy. The way intelligence services collect information, much of it through everyday conversation rather than hacking, makes it especially difficult for security teams to identify risks, according to retired senior intelligence officer Nicholas Eftimiades, who says he has trained more than 1,000 corporate security professionals. Some people inside Nvidia clearly knew parts of the picture. Nvidia’s top lawyer was engaged with the government’s Megaspeed inquiry more than a year ago, The New York Times reported earlier this week. (Nvidia has said it regularly contacts officials.) Reports about Huang’s relationships with employees suggest colleagues also knew of them, even if the behavior is not expressly forbidden by Nvidia’s code of conduct. The Times cited five Nvidia employees who said he was involved with a vice president who reported directly to him, and Reuters, citing two people, later reported a second relationship. What’s unclear is whether any of that reached security. Even if it had reached Nvidia’s security team, Eftimiades, who wrote Chinese Espionage Operations and Tactics in 2020, said a security team’s resources are often limited. For one thing, they’re often underfunded because, unlike some other cost centers, they don’t drive revenue. It’s astonishingly common for CEOs to answer a security team’s warnings with “not a nickel more than compliance,” he said. Many companies also define security overly narrowly, specialists say. In an opinion piece in The Hill, Don Aviv, CEO of the corporate investigations firm Interfor International, and author Jeremy Hurewitz, wrote, “Too many companies still approach security primarily as a matter of protecting facilities, preventing cyberattacks, and responding to physical threats.” The two argued that “[s]ecurity teams need to pay greater attention to insider threats, including the cultivation of executives and employees by foreign intelligence services, suspicious business relationships, conflicts of interest and attempts to obtain sensitive information through trusted personal contacts.” It would be surprising if Nvidia’s security team didn’t have a more expansive remit than most companies given its scale and business partners, but it’s possible. In fairness, some of it is simply beyond what any team can do. Speaking generally, not about Huang, Eftimiades offered a hypothetical in which a CEO complains that he can’t do something because “I’m fighting a board who doesn’t want to do this.” That tells an intelligence asset who the obstacle is. The service then asks, “Who’s the sticking point here?” and looks for ways into that person’s email and phone. What a rival intelligence service wants is often less technology than policy insight, including who’s pushing to change export rules and who the biggest blocker is. “Intel world tends to be like cancer,” he said. “Once it gets into the body, it looks to spread and looks to reach out.” The playbook isn’t new, Eftimiades added, “particularly for China.” Any executive dealing with the country “will tell you that they’ve been approached.” He said there are also “tons of diplomat stories” of U.S. diplomats walking into a hotel room to find a woman on the bed. He said what’s newer compared with Soviet era spying is the relationships these services cultivate now often last years, not weeks. Technology can augment that human intelligence, Eftimiades said, pointing to IMSI catchers as one example. The devices mimic a cell tower so that nearby phones connect to them. A basic version can cost about $1,000 and fit in a suitcase, he said, though government-grade models cost far more, and there were a couple of cases involving Chinese espionage where these factored in last year. Eftimiades says no one knows yet if the devices were used against Huang, whose phone was presumably hardened such that compromises could be detected, if not stopped altogether. But what Nvidia’s security team knew, and whether it could have acted on it, will only become clearer as the board’s independent investigation and federal inquiries proceed. In the meantime, Eftimiades said he hopes the whole episode is “a wake-up call” for U.S. industry, which he said is mostly “clueless” about China’s tactics. “We have lost trillions [of dollars] in intellectual property,” is his guess. “Whatever we think we’re doing isn’t working.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. articles.title: ‘Toy Story 5’ Producer Reflects On “Level Of Complexity” In Technology That Film Franchise Has Grown To Match With Curly Hair Tool Written For Blaze – Contenders L.A.
articles.description: As evidenced by the latest Toy Story film, technology is here to stay in toys and beyond. For producer Lindsey Collins, whose credits also include Disney/Pixar’s A Bug’s Life, Ratatouille, Finding Nemo and Turning Red, the key is balancing not overdeveloping the looks of animations in the films with moving them forward to suit advancements […]
articles.content: As evidenced by the latest Toy Story film, technology is here to stay in toys and beyond. For producer Lindsey Collins, whose credits also include Disney/Pixar‘s A Bug’s Life, Ratatouille, Finding Nemo and Turning Red, the key is balancing not overdeveloping the looks of animations in the films with moving them forward to suit advancements humanity has made and better capture certain details. “[We] try to keep it so we’re not evolving it so fast or so much that people are like, ‘This doesn’t feel like the Toy Story I recognize or I know,’ but also make sure that we’re keeping it so that we’re taking advantage of all the things we can do,” Collins said on a panel at Deadline’s Contenders Film Los Angeles event. “The technology just lets us do anything now. At the time, it was so restricted, like no hair or fur on the dog, or you couldn’t have you have tight clothing on everybody. One of the things that we’re really proud of is the character Blaze, who we all love, who’s the friend that ultimately comes as the gift at the end of the film. Curly hair is really hard. RELATED: ‘Toy Story 5’ Writer-Director Andrew Stanton Wants To Bring Nuance To The Conversation Between Kids & Technology Watch on Deadline “We’ve done curly hair before,” she added. “We’ve done it on Brave, but it is a technology that’s really hard to make look right. So we wrote a whole tool for the first time on this film to really capture the beauty and the gorgeousness of Blaze’s hair, and it took a ton of consultants internally to make sure: ‘Does it feel right? Does that look right? Does that feel like it looks natural to her?’ Those are the kinds of things that we try to do to take advantage of all this technology now to go, ‘Oh my gosh, we can now actually start to deliver a real sense of texture and softness,’ and that’s the kind of stuff that we would have cheated on all the other films.” Collins also marveled at the ability to create 50 Buzz Lightyears on 50 horses in the fifth film versus the possibility of rendering one in the 1999 original. RELATED: The 65 Movies That Have Made More Than $1 Billion At The Global Box Office “The level of complexity [of things] we can now do is pretty amazing,” she said. There was a version of the film’s ending where star character Jessie (voiced by Joan Cusack) meets an older version of her previous owner, Emily. “Because it was Jessie’s story, we knew we wanted her to reckon with the past with Emily, and there was a version at one point where she actually meets Emily, all grown up and old, and and we were like, “That’s a trip. OK, does that feel satisfying?’ As an audience, there was a lot of conversation around what’s going to be the satisfying gift for Jesse at the end,” Collins said. “Is it seeing Emily? Is it kind of understanding, getting the chance to kind of play with her again? These toys are like vampires; they don’t age. The rest of the world ages around them. We knew it had to be something that felt like it was the gift for her that she needed, the closure, and so that last scene with the buried treasure under the tree was the thing that probably took the longest to land.” RELATED: The 30 Highest-Grossing Animated Films Of All Time At The Global Box Office Collins closed the panel with reluctance that the films could eventually center AI, but she also didn’t rule out a next film to complete the “Bonnie years” trilogy just as Andy got three films. articles.content: Chris Pratt thinks it would be “awesome” to reunite with James Gunn for a fourth “Guardians of the Galaxy” film after the director announced his departure from DC Studios this week. Gunn and his co-chief, Peter Safran, were ousted from their positions on Nov. 9 following David Ellison’s Skydance merger in October. Marvel Studios alum Jeremy Latcham was announced as the new president and chief creative officer of DC Studios. Related Stories 'Wanted' Broadway Review: Dazzling Cast Can't Elevate the Musical’s Muted Narrative 'A Few Good Men' Review: Broadway Revival Breathes New Life Into Aaron Sorkin's Courtroom Classic The executive shuffle marks another setback for DC Studios, which has struggled to compete with the powerhouse that is Disney’s Marvel Cinematic Universe of late. But it opens a route for Gunn to return to the MCU, where he directed three “Guardians of the Galaxy” movies. Pratt recently told Moviezine that he would love to reunite with Gunn for a fourth film in the franchise. “That would be awesome. I love working with James. He’s the man,” Pratt said when asked about the possibility of making the film. “I haven’t had a chance to speak with him since that news came out yesterday…. It’s always tough because anytime something like this comes up, it could always become a headline.” He continued: “All I’ll say is I love James. He directed all three movies, and that’s pretty rare… so if he wanted to come back and bring it back, I would love that.” Pratt has starred as Star-Lord in the franchise across six films, with 2014’s “Guardians of the Galaxy,” “Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2,” “Avengers: Infinity War,” “Avengers: Endgame,” “Thor: Love and Thunder” and most recently in “Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3.” The Guardians of the Galaxy last graced the screens of viewers in 2023’s “Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3,” which promised via end-credits text that Star-Lord would return. Pratt has been vocal about his pitches to bring the character back and confirmed in October that the studio has taken “hard action” to make it happen.

articles.title: Elon Musk, other tech execs sign petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang
articles.description: The petition had attracted more than 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon.
articles.content: A petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate the company’s recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang appears to have attracted more than 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon. The petition website said the signers include 5,965 current Nvidia employees, 1,108 former employees, and 63,063 shareholders. Notable supporters include Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan. The petition states that its signers are “concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process” and demands that the board “bring him back while an independent investigation establishes the facts.” It also calls on the board to ensure a fair investigation and provide more information to the public. “Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice,” the petition says. Huang resigned on Thursday, four days after confessing to having an affair with a chip executive suspected by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy. The former CEO has agreed to testify before Congress, while news reports have also suggested that Huang engaged in multiple extramarital affairs. Nvidia appointed CFO Colette Kress as the company’s interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement. Nvidia’s stock price fell sharply through the week, while Huang’s departure is also expected to leave a big gap in AI industry funding. (Photo by Jan Sonnenmair/Getty Images)The number of confirmed measles cases across the U.S. this year has soared to 5,412 as of Nov. 12, more than double the 2,289 cases through all of 2025, according to the latest release of data from the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The trend has pushed the nation to lose its official “measles elimination status” after more than 25 years, according to news reports. “It’s pretty clear we’re hitting one grim milestone after the other,” Dr. Susan Kansagra, chief medical officer of the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials, a group representing local health officials, told Stateline. “It’s really, really just a hard time to see something that we know has been eliminated in the past, and to see this rapid growth that we have seen over these last two years.” The U.S. launched a national campaign to eliminate measles in the 1960s, around the time the first official measles vaccine was licensed to the public. In 1994, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a regional office of the World Health Organization representing states across the Americas, set a goal of ending the measles epidemic through a concerted vaccination effort, and by 2000 a panel of experts had concluded that the United States had eliminated measles from its population. This elimination status means that the nation is able to squash instances of measles transmission for 12 months or more. To reverse that status, measles must be spreading for 12 months or more – and now that’s where the U.S. is. A panel of experts at PAHO meeting in the past week to review cases has determined that the United States is no longer in elimination status, according to KFF Health News, which reported the news Nov. 14 citing researchers with direct knowledge of deliberations. The Wall Street Journal first reported the change Friday night. “And that means the disease has become what we call endemic again, meaning it’s just spreading in the community,” Katrine Wallace, an epidemiologist at the University of Illinois, Chicago School of Public Health, told Stateline. “I definitely blame it on the anti-vaccination kind of propaganda that’s been all over, and the lack of our (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services) really doing anything about these cases. “There’s not been a real push for vaccination efforts to counteract the 5,000 cases or something that we have now,” Wallace said. Measles is a highly contagious respiratory virus that leads to symptoms of fever, rash, and other serious health complications, including death, but is entirely avoidable through the two-dose MMR, or measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine. Children, who generally don’t get vaccinated before a year of age, are highly susceptible. But in his time in charge, U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has been an outspoken vaccine skeptic who opposes many vaccine mandates. His agency has called into question the safety and efficacy of vaccinations and recommended fewer vaccines for children. Many Republican-led states have ended vaccine mandates for their populations. Thirty-nine states now have MMR vaccination rates below 95% – the percentage necessary for herd immunity. According to the latest CDC data, measles cases have been reported this year across 47 states, plus the District of Columbia, and New York City. Among those cases, 58% of them, or 3,134, are among people under the age of 19. Among all cases, 96% are within people who are unvaccinated, and 11%, or 591 cases, have resulted in hospitalizations. The CDC has confirmed six measles-related deaths so far, though other investigations are continuing within individual states. Pennsylvania is experiencing a major outbreak, with 1,542 cases confirmed so far this year, including 37 cases since Nov. 9, according to the state’s health department. Just since Election Day, Pennsylvania has reported two “measles-associated” deaths, the most recent one announced Nov. 13. Two other deaths, in New York and Wisconsin, have been reported by state health agencies during the same period. “Revoking our elimination status doesn’t really change the reality on the ground, right? We all know, you know, that we have measles in our community,” said Dr. Ali Khan, a medical epidemiologist and dean of the College of Public Health at the University of Nebraska Medical Center. “Measles has always been the sort of ultimate stress test for public health infrastructure,” Khan said in an interview Friday. “And we’re failing that test … if you can’t get people vaccinated, that says something about the quality of your health system.” Khan said the real message behind the potential revocation of the elimination status is that the nation’s leaders desperately need to fund and promote public health infrastructure in communities, so that people can protect themselves. Kansagra, who works with local and state health departments, said it’s particularly worrisome that major federal public health grant programs and pandemic-era funds are expiring at the end of next year. “That type of core infrastructure support for public health is so important because these are exactly the types of threats that public health is dealing with and working to respond to,” Kansagra said. Wallace is hopeful on the heels of the 2026 midterm elections in November that Democrats, especially ones steeped in public health like Michigan Sen. Abdul El-Sayed, a medical doctor, can change the direction of the country’s public health policy in time to prevent more death and spread of disease. “We’re voting these people in,” Wallace said. “So it seems like the country is moving towards wanting to rein this in.” Stateline reporter Shalina Chatlani can be reached at schatlani@stateline.org. James Gunn is setting the record straight on rumors surrounding the future of Man of Tomorrow following the announcement that he and Peter Safran will step down from their leadership roles at DC Studios. Following the announcement, rumors have circulated alleging that Skydance plans to make changes to Man of Tomorrow, including potentially removing certain characters and making significant alterations to the film. Gunn took to Threads to address the claims, denying that Skydance had even seen the movie. “There are a lot of untrue rumors going around, but one of them is that Skydance has seen Man of Tomorrow and that all sorts of sweeping changes are being made,” he wrote. “No one from Skydance has even seen the movie — the only people that have are Peter Safran and a very small trusted group of friends and family. So any stories around this narrative are false.” Related Stories Business HBO Max-Paramount+ Bundle Targeted by Subscribers in Lawsuit Challenging Megamerger Movies Skyler Gisondo Reacts to James Gunn, Peter Safran's DC Exits: "There's a Lot I Still Don't Know" Man of Tomorrow, the sequel to 2025’s Superman, stars David Corenswet as Clark Kent/Superman, Nicholas Hoult, Lars Eidinger, Rachel Brosnahan, Skyler Gisondo, Sara Sampaio, Isabela Merced, Nathan Fillion, Edi Gathegi and Adria Arjona also star. Principal photography wrapped in August, and the film is currently scheduled to hit theaters July 9. Earlier this week, Gisondo, who is also reprising his role as Daily Planet photographer Jimmy Olsen in HBO Max’s The People v. Gorilla Grodd, shared his reaction to the leadership change with The Hollywood Reporter. “It’s really sad to see them go. They really changed all of our lives. Gorilla Grodd are in post-production, with the latter having wrapped filming in October. Gunn was also working on a third Superman movie before the leadership change. Former Marvel executive Jeremy Latcham is set to take over as DC Studios’ president and chief creative officer on Dec. 1. articles.content: Village employees clear debris left behind by historic ice storms in Wolverine Monday, April 1.The U.S. Department of Energy has issued another emergency order forcing a West Michigan coal-fired power plant to remain open. The J.H. Campbell plant, which sits on the lakeshore in Ottawa County, was originally scheduled to be shut down in the summer of 2025. But the DOE has repeatedly ordered Consumers Energy, which operates the plant, to stay open, citing an energy emergency.The state of Michigan sued to overturn the order. In September, a federal judge sided with the state, concluding that the federal government “exceeded its statutory authority.” The Department is now appealing that decision.The previous order keeping the J.H. Campbell plant open was scheduled to expire on Saturday. Late Friday, the DOE issued a new order, which it says is valid for another 90 days.Consumers Energy has filed to reclaim the costs of keeping the plant open. If granted, that would mean the costs would be passed on to Consumers customers in the form of rate hikes. In September, the Michigan Attorney General’s office said the additional costs of operating J.H. Campbell had reached $295 million.“By forcing its continued operation, DOE tried a never-before-used tactic to illegally prop up the aging J.H. Campbell coal plant that nobody asked to keep, sticking ratepayers with a bill for a facility that should have been retired more than a year ago,” Attorney General Dana Nessel said in a statement.In its most recent emergency order, the DOE continued to argue that the power grid in Michigan faced the possibility of shortages during periods of peak electricity demand and the winter season."President Trump and the Energy Department remain committed to doing everything in our power to stop power outages for American families and businesses," said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright.The current emergency order will expire Feb. 12, 2027.

Country Day survives and advances past Lutheran North for regional title
articles.content: MACOMB TWP. – Sometimes it’s a play or two that can make the difference in advancing or going home during the state tournament. After not even making the postseason field the past three seasons, the Yellowjackets found a way to rally past host Macomb Lutheran North 21-13 in a Division 4 regional finals clash to advance to the state semifinals for the 21st time in school history. Country Day (9-3) will face defending state champion Dearborn Divine Child (11-1) in the Final Four at a neutral site on Nov. 21. Lutheran North finishes the season with a 10-2 overall record. “I’ve coached in a lot of games like this over the years,” smiled veteran Detroit Country Day coach Dan MacLean. “We had to make plays and the guys battled hard. That was a very good high school football team. Lutheran North made some plays too and they have some really nice players. We just made some great plays to come back and win this football game. “It’s all about surviving and advancing,” added McLean, who announced earlier this season that this campaign would be his last. Down 13-12, Country Day had a pass picked off but it was later rules that there was a pass interference call that allowed the Yellowjackets to retain the ball. Junior Jacob Patton later had a 58-yard run down to the Lutheran North 3 and ran it into the end zone on the next play to put DCD up for good at 18-13 with 8:06 remaining in the game. The two-point conversion failed. Country Day was able to get the ball back and drive the ball downfield before senior Mitchel Hamway booted a 17-yard field goal to put his team up eight with 1:39 remaining in the contest. “I know we were down, but we fought back to win this game,” smiled Patton. “We fought and I played like a dawg. We played tough and found a way.” Patton was a workhorse with 30 carries for 175 yards tor Country Day. Sophomore Carson McGuire was 11-for-16 passing for 159 yards and junior Atlas Amezcua had four catches for 49 yards. Senior Joe Avolio had 22 carries for 138 yards to pace Lutheran North. Junior Owen VanderVlucht finished 8-for-17 passing for 75 yards, while senior Charlie Bates had three catches for 33 yards for Mustangs. Country Day finally broke the scoreless stalemate when McGuire connected with Rhys Kenney for an 18-yard touchdown strike, but a penalty pushed back the extra point attempt and the Yellowjackets misfired on the play to settle for a 6-0 advantage with 33 seconds left in the first half. That lead was erased when Lutheran North’s Bates returned the kickoff 92 yards for the score and Aidan Vermiglio made his extra point to give the Mustangs a 7-6 advantage. North also recovered the onside kick on the next play but ran out of time trying to put more points on the board. Country responded with 8:35 left in the third quarter when McGuire connected with a streaking Amezcua down the left sideline for a 12-7 lead. The two-point conversion failed again as the Yellowjackets settled for the five-point advantage. Lutheran North was able to go ahead one final time at 13-12 when Avolio scored on a 6-yard run. The Mustangs’ went for two and it was originally called pass interference against Country Day, but the flag was picked up and left it a one-point game. Lutheran North tied a school record with 10 wins this season and just their second district championship the previous week but couldn’t generate enough offense in extending its season. “We still had a great season,” noted first-year Lutheran North head coach Brad Morris. “We scored the second most points in Lutheran North history. These kids worked hard to get us to this point. We just came up short. We had the lead but Country Day found a way to come back. That’s how it goes sometimes.” Photo gallery of the Detroit Country Day vs. Macomb Lutheran North D-4 regional finals football game

articles.title: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
articles.description: From Apple's repeatedly delayed Siri AI to OpenAI's messy "super app" launch, here's a look at the AI projects that shut down or missed expectations.
articles.content: Last month, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching. More recently, privacy-focused AI assistant Ollie announced its shutdown a few weeks ago. Aside from Character.ai and Ollie, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand. The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry. Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “super app.” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.” The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after, bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back. That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT. The company did the same thing with Operator, an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images. We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora, which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026. When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively. However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs. This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16. Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow. Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai was a consumer AI app that let people chat with customizable bots, many of them modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. It raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. Then, the next year, Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring its founders back into its orbit, leaving the startup to carry on without them. Character.ai has run into a lot of trouble over the years. Families have sued, alleging the chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm, and Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized use of its characters. Character.ai barred under-18 users from open-ended chats late last year and agreed to settle several of the suits, along with Google, in early 2026. But it wasn’t enough. The company filed for bankruptcy in early October, citing legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. In an ironic twist, Disney is now the opening bidder, offering $20 million for a license to some of its intellectual property. The app is still running during the process, and the sale is expected to wrap up by late November or early December. Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August 2026. The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product. Ollie launched in June 2026 as one of the first mainstream apps to achieve SOC 2, a privacy compliance standard. Similar to the other family-focused agents, the idea behind Ollie was that families already have the information they need, but it lives across school messages, calendars, task lists, and group chats. Ollie aimed to bring those pieces together and keep them in sync. It kept track of calendars, emails, reminders, tasks, and other household details, then delivered relevant information to users through text. However, the app faced a very common challenge: keeping up with heavyweights like Muse and Instinct. Co-founder and CEO Bill Lennon revealed the app would shut down on November 6, citing difficulties like being unable to stand out, failing to grow, and not raising enough capital. Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s Recall feature was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history. Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate backlash over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. Microsoft delayed the feature for nearly a year, giving the company time to rethink its security and privacy protections. Even after a redesign, the controversy hasn’t gone away. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could extract and display data that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem. Notion Mail launched in April 2025 as an AI-focused email product designed to help users organize and automate their inboxes. However, the company noticed its users were using separate AI agents to handle their email inboxes instead. As a result, Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on September 22. The Humane AI Pin is probably one of the most well-known failures in AI hardware. Designed to provide AI features through a wearable device rather than a traditional smartphone, Humane raised $230 million from investors and garnered significant attention. But the product struggled mightily with performance, and the situation worsened when Humane warned customers to stop using its charging case because of a potential battery fire risk. Humane then shut down its AI Pin business in February 2025, with most of the company’s assets acquired by HP for $116 million. The Rabbit R1 was another heavily hyped AI device. Unveiled at CES in January 2024, the AI companion was designed to perform tasks on behalf of its owner. Rabbit said it had sold 100,000 units shortly after launch. However, strong initial sales didn’t mean it was a strong product. Early reviews described the device as unfinished, with unreliable performance and a limited number of useful integrations. The company hasn’t given up, though. It has continued updating the R1, positioning it as a computer controller capable of performing agentic tasks. It also recently announced a new hardware project, dubbed “Project Cyberdeck,” aimed at creating a portable device built for vibe-coding. Huxe was an AI audio app, built by former developers of Google’s NotebookLM, that turned written information into conversational, podcast-style audio. The company shut down in May 2026, partly as larger platforms began offering similar experiences to large existing audiences. For instance, Spotify has been expanding its own AI-powered audio tools. Yupp was an interesting AI product: a free playground that allowed users to compare responses from hundreds of AI models side by side. Users could also vote on responses and earn cryptocurrency through the platform. At its peak, the platform let users test more than 800 models, including from companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. But according to its founders, Yupp never achieved strong enough product-market fit to survive. The platform shut down in March 2026. Figgs AI operated from 2023 to 2024, letting users create and interact with customizable AI characters for role-play and storytelling. The platform reportedly drew more than 1 million users, but its developers said keeping the service free became too expensive to sustain, and they shut it down. articles.content: Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life. Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman. That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. OpenAI has since restructured entirely. But it’s worth remembering what Helen and the board were supposed to do: OpenAI’s nonprofit board existed specifically to make sure the company didn’t betray its mission to build safe AI by prioritizing profit and growth over safety. When the board actually tried to pull the lever, that accountability mechanism broke, and here we are. --- [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/24792604/The_Verge_Decoder_Tileart.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. --- Now, the question of AI safety is everywhere. This summer, AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic broke out of their testing environments and hacked real companies. The CEOs of these frontier labs have since called for a slowdown and asked Washington for help, but the White House’s answer was a voluntary accord — one that relies in part on the kind of board accountability that failed at OpenAI. Anthropic is also about to go public, which will put a whole new set of market pressures on OpenAI’s biggest competitor. Helen has seen up close what happens when safety commitments run headlong into commercial incentives. And as she put it to me, if our hopes for the future depend on any one person being trustworthy, we’re in big trouble. So we talked about what we might do instead: what the labs are actually trying to build, whether AI alignment is a problem that can be solved, and what a smarter approach to AI regulation might look like. That includes how to think about China, which is the issue that looms large in every policy conversation about AI right now — especially now after the Jensen Huang affair. Just for clarity, Helen and I talked before Nvidia opened its investigation and Jensen ultimately resigned, so you won’t hear us talk about that directly. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Helen Toner, the executive director of CSET, on the future of AI safety. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Helen Toner, you’re the executive director for the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. Welcome to Decoder. Thanks so much. Great to be here. I have wanted to talk to you for 10 million years. I am so excited you’re here. You’ve been involved in a lot of AI safety and ethics ideas for a long time. You were obviously on the board of OpenAI during what everyone has come to call “the blip.” Now, you’re talking a lot about AI safety, about which I have 10 million questions. But let’s just start at the start. You run the Center for Security and Emerging Technology, people call it CSET. What is CSET? It’s awesome to be here. I’m really excited to talk to you as well. CSET is a team inside Georgetown, but we’re really not academics. We’re about 50 people and have been going since 2019. Basically in 2019, a group of us decided that there was a lot happening and a lot of emerging technologies that were becoming very relevant in the national security space, and the security space more broadly,. And some policymakers who had very important jobs did not have the time or the expertise to get across what was going on with those emerging technologies. Already at the top of our list in 2019 was AI. Basically our mission is to do analysis that is really rigorous, but also actionable, for policymakers and analysis that is both grounded in the technology and grounded in real national security expertise and understanding and issues. We produce long reports. We go do short briefings on those long reports to busy policymakers. We have a big data team that helps us do our research. We do all kinds of cool stuff. Can I just ask about the dynamics of that for one minute? You and I are talking the day after the midterm elections in the United States of America, and there was a big blue wave. There’s a lot of polling that says the number one issue is corruption. We’re going to throw the bums out. We’re going to start over and get rid of these corrupt guys. The AI industry, and the tech industry, has flooded a bunch of money into politics. And then somewhere next to that is, “Oh, there’s a bunch of well-meaning researchers who are going to show up and tell you how it actually works and what the real risks are.” It just occurs to me that maybe people don’t believe that’s effective anymore, that the money and the corruption and the AI CEO standing next to Trump have completely outweighed the well-meaning, sincere, “here are the actual problems” research that you do. What is that dynamic actually like? It’s a reasonable concern to have, and there are definitely some spaces where money just absolutely overwhelms everything. I’m Australian. I didn’t grow up in the US, and so the amount of money in US elections is pretty mind-blowing to me, but there are limits to what money can do. AI is a great example. In this election, there were just unbelievable amounts of money being thrown at candidates, at messages, at opposition research. There was all kinds of astroturfing on Twitter, and some very strange things trying to get anyone who talked about AI governance, regulation, safety, any of those words thrown out or not elected. It turns out to have really not worked very well. I think the reason that it didn’t work very well is one, this is an issue that voters increasingly care about. And two, also interestingly, it’s an issue that is pretty bipartisan at this point. What we see in our work is that there is a real thirst among policymakers for high-quality information. articles.content: Tesla is doubling, or perhaps tripling down on its bold claims of an autonomous future with the offer to “select customers” to purchase a Cybercab for “personal use.” But the gilded, steering-wheel-free two-seater will “only be available in supported service areas” — meaning you’ll only be able to buy one if you live in one of the cities where Tesla currently operates its Robotaxi service. The price of a Cybercab is listed at $29,990, plus a mandatory $299-a-month “Autonomy Subscription.” Tesla’s Robotaxi account on X announced the new offer, including screenshots of the order page and the invite email. But don’t expect a fleet of personally owned Cybercabs to suddenly materialize on public roads: “Initial availability is limited,” the invitation email warns. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/HXCrorcbwAAQTq0_569a68.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/HXCr4I4bYAA8lrS.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/11/HXCr4Iza4AErLOW.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Tesla began offering rides in the Cybercab as part of its Model Y-powered Robotaxi service in Austin in September. The company now has 278 Cybercabs in operation, representing approximately 40 percent of its fleet, according to the crowd-sourced Robotaxi Tracker. The inclusion of a mandatory $299/month subscription is sure to rankle some fans who may have dreamed of cruising around in a $30,000 driverless Tesla, as originally promised by Tesla CEO Elon Musk when he first introduced the Cybercab in 2024. Musk made no mention of the Autonomy Subscription at that event, though it shouldn’t come as too much of a surprise given the $99/month fee Tesla currently charges for its Full Self-Driving (FSD) feature. Still, that money adds up over time. Over a standard 5-year ownership period, the mandatory $299/month fee adds $17,940 to the sticker price (even with the first month included), bringing the real baseline cost to roughly $47,600 before taxes, charging, and insurance — more than a brand-new Model 3 or Model Y that you can actually drive anywhere in the country. Unlike a standard Tesla where canceling FSD just reverts the car to manual driving, canceling the $299/month Autonomy Subscription renders the Cybercab completely unusable on public roads because there is no manual fallback. In effect, the car becomes a brick. Additionally, Tesla says that buyers will have to put down a $1,000 non-refundable deposit just to get in line for a December delivery window that isn’t guaranteed. One of the biggest selling points of Musk’s 2024 “We, Robot” pitch was that regular people could buy a Cybercab and add it to Tesla’s Robotaxi network to earn passive income while they sleep or work. But the order terms explicitly prohibit owners from using the vehicle for commercial purposes — meaning no Uber, no DoorDash, and no putting it on Tesla’s own Robotaxi network to offset the $299/month fee. Tesla AI chief Ashok Elluswamy has floated Q2 2027 as a possible target for letting customer cars join the network, so early buyers are paying full freight with zero way to monetize the car. Moreover, Tesla only has to give you 30 days’ warning before raising the price. If they update the rules and you keep using the service, you automatically agree to the new terms. Also, if you cancel — or if Tesla suspends your access — you won’t get a partial refund for the rest of the month you already paid for. Of course, that’s just the fine print. On X, Tesla CEO Elon Musk was promising a much wider rollout, subject — of course — to “regulatory approval.” Musk frequently frames regulatory approval as the primary external bottleneck holding back his robotaxi timelines as a way to shift focus away from Tesla’s technological shortcomings. (For what it’s worth, he also called his own company’s $299/month Autonomy Subscription “too high,” arguing that it should actually be $115/month or closer to Tesla’s $99/month Full Self-Driving subscription.) But Musk seemed more focused on taunting YouTuber Marques Brownlee, who promised to shave his head if Tesla delivered a Cybercab for under $30,000 before 2027, than answering any of the litany of safety and liability questions raised by this offer. (For his part, Brownlee says he thinks his hair is safe.) For starters, how does Tesla plan on selling a vehicle that doesn’t comply with current Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards that require traditional controls like steering wheels and pedals? Tesla says the Autonomy Subscription covers autonomous driving, maintenance, and towing, but explicitly excludes auto insurance. The company hasn’t explained how personal auto insurers will underwrite a car with no human driver, or how liability is split between the owner and Tesla if the vehicle causes an accident while operating autonomously. Nor has Tesla disclosed how it selects invited buyers or how many units are earmarked for private sale versus its internal fleet. Then there is the small matter of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration already opening a formal audit into how Tesla self-certified a vehicle without a steering wheel, pedals, or side mirrors. Tesla submitted its legal justification to NHTSA in October, requested that the entire response be kept confidential, and is now taking customer deposits while NHTSA’s ruling is still pending. Which means early buyers aren’t just paying $47,600 for a geofenced car they aren’t allowed to drive — they’re putting down non-refundable cash on a vehicle the federal government hasn’t even decided is street-legal.

articles.content: East Lansing officials said they will be cracking down on couch burning after dozens of fire calls during the night of Michigan State University’s win over rival University of Michigan. It was the first win since 2021 for the Spartans, and couch burning has a long history in East Lansing. An East Lansing Fire Department truck leaves for a call immediately after a news conference on Nov. 13, where city officials talked about curbing couch fires in the city, related to Michigan State University events. Photo by Mike Ellis/City Pulse East Lansing Fire Chief John Newman said there were around 50 nuisance fires that night. “They are not celebrations,” Newman said, during a Friday news conference at the city’s fire station on Abbott Road. “Setting fires in our streets, alleys and yars is reckless criminal behavior that puts lives, property and our first responders at serious risk. The real world consequnce of this activity was an immediate dangerous strain on our entire emergency response system.” A backlog at Ingham County 911 Central Dispatch, directly affecting response time elsewhere in the county, Newman said, and potentially for life-threatening situations. i’ve responded to hundreds, hundreds of these in my career,” he said, “these nuisance fires associated with a win, a loss or some other reason. They’re not fun. They’re not fun. Frankly, they’re idiotic and super dangerous.” An East Lansing Fire Department truck leaves for a call immediately after a news conference on Nov. 13, where city officials talked about curbing couch fires in the city, related to Michigan State University events. Photo by Mike Ellis/City Pulse He said the Sheriff’s Office plans to put resources into solving the fires and preventing them. There can be five, 10 or even 15 calls at one time, he said. That ties up dispatchers and responders. Officials said they plan to solve some of the fires and make prosecutions, and work with Michigan State University for further discipline for any students involved. Removing combustable material ahead of events and other efforts will be part of the process, officials said. Deb Haaland breaks political barriers as Native women in her home community face hurdles
articles.content: N.M. (AP) — On the morning of a Laguna Pueblo village’s annual Feast Day, Ashley Sarracino knelt in her family home holding clothespins between her teeth. She straightened her niece’s black cotton manta, a traditional one-shouldered dress, and tied a sash around her waist. On these days, Sarracino is a caretaker, dressing relatives for the harvest dance and helping feed up to 150 guests. And as a former member of the pueblo council, she knows how to balance those traditional responsibilities with official duties. “To me, those things aren’t in conflict at all,” she said. Yet even as another Laguna Pueblo woman, former U.S. Interior Secretary Deb Haaland, is set to become the first Native American woman state governor, women with leadership aspirations such as Sarracino say they are swimming upstream in their Pueblo communities. Sarracino said she was forced off the council after alleging she was paid less because she was a woman, a claim pueblo officials deny. In some of the 19 pueblos in New Mexico, including Laguna, tribal law and customs do not allow women to hold top government positions. Haaland told The Associated she was once nominated to serve on her pueblo council but did not make it past a primary. She quipped it was “easier to raise $1 million and run for Congress” than succeed in Pueblo politics. “It’s still a man’s world in a lot of Pueblo communities, and certainly in mine,” she said. Sarracino was offered a road map familiar to ambitious young Native people: Leave the reservation to get an education, then return home to serve your community. She built a career in nonprofit work and political organizing, including as chair of her county’s Democratic Party. In 2022, Sarracino was nominated by a pueblo elder to run for council secretary. She finished second, but was appointed to the post after a resignation. “Finally I had an opportunity to use my skills to help my own community,” she said. While reviewing budget documents, Sarracino discovered she was being paid $14,000 less than her male predecessor. She asked the pueblo governor for an explanation, sparking a bitter dispute that would end her tenure on council. The council says Sarracino was paid less because she lacked experience and that she abandoned her post. But Sarracino insists she was ousted and that the pay discrepancy reflects sexist attitudes embedded in tribal law. Since 1996, the pueblo’s election code has allowed women to run for council treasurer and secretary, but it does not explicitly allow them to serve as governor or lieutenant governor. Its constitution, last amended in 2012, refers to the governor as “he” and “him.” Sarracino’s dispute landed in tribal court but was dismissed this year on sovereign immunity grounds and she’s exhausted her appeals. The case took a toll on her mental health. She said it’s been bittersweet to watch Haaland make political history. “We all know she would never have the same opportunity here,” she said. Yet Haaland’s ascent could help change attitudes at home. Emily Hunt, who became Laguna Pueblo’s first female elected official in the late ’90s with legal help from Haaland, believes the pueblo will someday nominate a woman governor. “Whether I’ll see it in my lifetime, I don’t know,” Hunt said. Some pueblos retain traditional theocracies, with government roles appointed by ceremonial elders and reserved for men. Charlotte Little, a citizen of San Felipe Pueblo, said women in those communities hold esteemed roles of their own. A New Mexico state representative, Little never aspired to lead at home. “It’s about respecting the culture that I come from,” she said. Other pueblos, under federal pressure in the 1930s, adopted secular constitutions and elections. That includes Isleta Pueblo, where in 1986 Verna Teller overcame a contentious legal battle to become its first and only woman governor. Council incumbents attempted unsuccessfully to strike Teller’s name from the ballot, arguing a woman could not hold office under Isleta law. She won in a landslide. Now in her 70s, Teller blames colonization for the patriarchy that she says persists in traditionally matrilineal Pueblo communities. “When the Spaniards and the Catholics came here, they didn’t want to deal with the clan mothers. They threw women in the back seat,” Teller said. “That has turned into this paternalistic attitude that men have to be in charge.” That’s not the case at every pueblo. At Pojoaque Pueblo, where council positions are open to all and candidates don’t need to be nominated, women have held all four executive positions since 2021. Haaland is the most prominent among a wave of Pueblo women who have found success in mainstream politics, from school boards to state government and U.S. Congress. She encouraged Pueblo women to look beyond their home communities for opportunities. “We need more Native women everywhere,” she told The AP. Sarracino has not ruled out a future pueblo council run and, after attending Haaland’s election night celebration, now sees a potential path in state politics. On Feast Day, as her family home sprang to life with visitors, Sarracino greeted friends and relatives with hugs, refilled their iced teas and later made sure they went home with oven bread and fruit pie. She watched with pride as her nieces giggled over plates of enchiladas, their hands white with ceremonial clay from the morning’s dances. She is planning her next move with those girls in mind. “That’s the reason I couldn’t just let it go,” she said. “Because I know they’re coming up behind me.” This story is published through the Global Indigenous Reporting Network at The Associated Press.

James Webb telescope finds ice older than the star it orbits
articles.description: Radiation and collisions reshape the planetary building materials.
articles.content: Beta Pictoris is a young star, roughly 20 million years old, and located about 64 light-years away from Earth. It is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rubble where planets are still forming—astronomers have already found three. In a new Science study, a team led by Sarah Betti, an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, used the James Webb Space Telescope to look for ice in this disk. Researchers found both water and carbon dioxide ice. The water ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and it is mixed with carbon dioxide in roughly the same proportions we see in comets of our own Solar System. This suggests ingredients necessary to form water-rich worlds might be common around young stars. The missing ice Beta Pictoris is one of the best studied stars in the sky. Its disk was among the first ever imaged, back in 1984, and we see it almost exactly edge-on, which makes it a natural laboratory for studying how planetary systems grow. It's what astronomers call a debris disk, where the dust is constantly replenished by collisions among comets and planetesimals, small bodies that are the building blocks of planets.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Winemakers are learning that conservation can be good for business
articles.description: Healthy soils, native plants, and fewer chemicals are helping vineyards adapt.
articles.content: More than 500 vineyards are scattered across the slopes and valleys of South Africa’s Western Cape, one of the world’s most biologically diverse landscapes. The region produces about 90 percent of South Africa’s wine, but winemakers there are increasingly struggling with drought, excessive heat and erratic rainfall. Temperatures in the region have risen 1.5 to 2 times faster than the global average over the past five decades. And extreme storms have become more intense as climate variability increases. The late 2010s brought a significant challenge for winemakers, as three years of severe drought placed vineyards under intense stress and reduced grape production. As climate variability places increasing pressure on grape production, many wine producers are building on sustainability measures that have long been part of vineyard management.Read full article Comments

articles.title: How a historic El Niño might spare northern Michigan from a harsh winter
articles.description: This story is made possible through a partnership between Interlochen Public Radio and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization. Northern Michigan may see a mild, drier winter this year because of a strengthening El Niño in the Pacific Ocean. The natural climate pattern happens about every four to seven years, when sea surface temperatures in […]
articles.content: People on a frozen Grand Traverse Bay in winter 2026. (Photo credit: Vivian La/IPR News)This story is made possible through a partnership between Interlochen Public Radio and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization. Northern Michigan may see a mild, drier winter this year because of a strengthening El Niño in the Pacific Ocean. The natural climate pattern happens about every four to seven years, when sea surface temperatures in the Central Pacific remain above average for several months in a row. The extra warmth fuels changes in atmospheric patterns, affecting Michiganders thousands of miles away. While this year’s El Niño is on track to break records, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, most of the Midwest may be spared from some of the more dramatic impacts forecasted elsewhere in the country, such as a busy hurricane season for Hawaii and the Pacific Islands or a wetter Northeast. How will El Niño impact the rest of the country? See a region-by-region breakdown from Grist. Impacts are so variable because changes to how air moves around the globe, and its impacts on weather, depend a lot on timing, location and local seasons. Here’s what to know about El Niño’s impacts in northern Michigan. What effects are we already seeing? El Niño shifts the location of the jet streams across the US — the fast-moving bands of air located at the same height that airplanes fly — keeping the cold Arctic air that typically comes into the Great Lakes region this time of year farther north. “We don’t have a nice dipping trough of a jet stream to bring those cold air masses down over us,” said Daria Kluver, a professor at Central Michigan University’s Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences. That’s led to a warmer and drier fall than average for much of northern Michigan, according to Sean Christensen, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Gaylord. October temperatures in the region were at least 4 degrees higher than average, according to the National Weather Service. Gaylord temperatures last month were 6.6 degrees above average, while Traverse City was 4.7 degrees warmer. How will El Niño impact winter in northern Michigan? El Niño peaks in the US before the end of the year, but effects linger for several months. In northern Michigan, above-average temperatures will continue throughout the winter, experts said. During past strong El Niño events, winter temperatures in northern Michigan ranged from 2 to 6 degrees above average, according to the weather service office in Gaylord. The region will also likely see less snow than average, including lake effect areas. Warmer temperatures may limit lake effect impacts. “Whether you find that good or bad maybe depends on what you do for winter recreation,” she said. What other factors will shape the region’s winter besides El Niño? Kluver said El Niño doesn’t rule out chances of precipitation in the form of rain or ice, even if there’s less snow. But that will depend on other dynamics like how much sea ice is in the Arctic or atmospheric patterns in the Atlantic Ocean, she said. “El Niño is not the only player here, but it is a really strong signal,” Kluver said. How does El Niño impact ice on the Great Lakes? A warmer-than-average winter could reduce the amount of ice cover on the Great Lakes, providing additional moisture and moderating temperatures throughout the region. Ice thickness sampling on Saginaw Bay in February 2025. (Courtesy of Ayumi Fujisake-Manome) In three of the four recent very strong El Niño events, ice cover on each of the lakes was lower. And the timing of peak ice occurred earlier in the year, according to the US Geological Survey. El Niño can fuel lower ice levels, but comes as the Great Lakes are already seeing less ice because of climate change, from warmer winters and fewer blasts of cold Arctic air. The changes in ice cover could impact Great Lakes economies, recreation, and the ecosystems that depend on it — such as less ice fishing, an extended shipping season across the lakes and more shoreline erosion. What makes this a “super” El Niño? “Super” is not a technical term. But it does speak to the likelihood of a “historic event” that would surpass the current El Niño records going back to 1950, according to the weather service’s Climate Prediction Center. The center forecasts an 83% chance of a “strong to very strong” El Niño through the start of 2027. Ocean temperatures over the last three months tracked by NOAA have averaged 2 degrees Celsius warmer than usual. At this same time during the last strong El Niño event in 2015, temperatures were 1.8 degrees Celsius. That strength has already contributed to weather extremes in other parts of the country. In the Southwest, above-average rainfall has exacerbated flooding. Across the world, drought in the Amazon is fueling massive fires. How is climate change affecting El Niño? The impacts of climate change on El Niño are a growing body of research, and some experts say it can be hard to tease out the two. But the above-average ocean temperatures from El Niño are happening against the backdrop of increasingly warm waters as they absorb the excess heat from burning fossil fuels, said Richard Rood, professor emeritus at the University of Michigan who studies climate change. There’s been enough warming that NOAA started using a new El Niño measurement this year that factors in some of that background warming, called the Relative Oceanic Niño Index. It’s an index that uses three-month averages of ocean temperatures and is already used by weather services in Australia and New Zealand. Increased ocean temperatures — even temporarily from El Niño — drive changes in the atmosphere that might not be seen for several years, Rood said. “The patterns are changing as the planet is warming,” Rood said. “We are in this pattern of non-stationarity.” This reporting is made possible by the Northern Michigan Journalism Collaborative, led by Bridge Michigan and Interlochen Public Radio, and funded by Press Forward Northern Michigan.
