Opinion: We should delay GM, Bedrock’s plans for Detroit’s Riverfront
articles.description: "Detroiters always deserve more than we get, and this deal is a continuation of the asymmetrical and inequitable balance that is development in Detroit."
articles.content: I am one of two elected members of the Neighborhood Advisory Committee (NAC), tasked with negotiating the Community Benefits Agreement (CBA) for the Renaissance Center and RiverEast project. I was also the sole no vote against the presented CBA for many reasons. While I could critique the many issues with the CBO process, such as the NAC having no policy assistance, having multiple marathon sessions lasting eight-plus hours in an effort to respond to the developer quicker than they responded back to us, and the fact that we (regular community members) sat across the table from a panel of corporate attorneys from General Motors Co. and Bedrock, I voted no because this deal did not properly speak to Detroiters. I voted no because Detroiters always deserve more than we get, and this deal is a continuation of the asymmetrical and inequitable balance that is development in Detroit. Of course the Renaissance Center needs to be reimagined. The owner, GM, has moved out, and the other tenants are following behind. With just a Marriott and a couple of restaurants remaining in the complex, any property owner would be planning what to do next. Based on GM and Bedrock’s engagement with the community, one would assume that this development would be the pinnacle of co-design. It would be a metric for how public-private partnerships should exist. However, no matter how loud the community chanted, we were offered only the same tangible benefits; nothing about the project changed. TeRon Haynes, Jr. By dollar amount, the public money, our tax money, is the second-largest financial contributor to the project, and our money is being spent almost solely to demolish our city’s most notable landmark. Then, throughout the project’s life, GM and Bedrock will get paid back with our sales taxes, and these mega-corporations can contribute their equity at their leisure. The project is operating within a 10-year timeline, but it should be noted that the deadlines are verbal and not contractual. The risk is too great to gamble with both our money and prime waterfront real estate. To be clear, there is no commitment to build the marina or the movie theater or the observation deck outlined in the benefits agreement; rather, these are verbal commitments with nonbinding language. There is no contribution to public transit even though the project advertises connectivity. The people also demanded it. We have seen no breakdown of construction costs and no range for operating costs. No one has seen a pro forma (the project’s projected cash flows) that is outside the deal. There are no interior images and no construction documents. It is almost as though we are co-signing a huge construction deal without any plans. We should not have to take “trust me” for an answer. From the first public presentation of the Renaissance Center and RiverEast project, we were told the towers were coming down. When residents asked why, the answer was simple: just accept it. That was non-negotiable, but everything else would still be on the table for our Community Benefits Agreement. Over the course of nine weekly CBO meetings, we learned that, in reality, there was a lot that was off-limits. Even though we presented a robust initial draft, our offer was countered with the creation of a nonprofit entity that committed to none of our demands and only generated more unanswered questions. Because the NAC ultimately did not have the proper resources or time to research and negotiate a proper CBA, City Council must demand due diligence. The icon, the barrier, the fortress, the symbol — whatever the Renaissance Center was and will become, we need to take a closer look at the details in this proposal. For that reason, I request that the City Council delay this vote to give this project the due diligence it deserves. Let me make one thing clear: I am for union labor, and I am for development in Detroit, and the council does not have to reject this project. It is not a radical position to ask the council not to sign a blank check. It is what any investor asks before writing a $548 million check. A few more weeks of due diligence now could be the only way we protect our riverfront for the next thirty years. TeRon Haynes, Jr. is a military veteran, Detroit resident, and community organizer in Detroit and Southeast Michigan. He advocates for social equity across multiple disciplines, primarily through the lens of public health and safety.

articles.title: South Sudan postpones first national elections again, to February 2027
articles.description: South Sudan postpones first national elections again, to February 2027 AP News South Sudan pushes back elections as violence threatens fragile peace DW.com South Sudan’s National Election, Its First, Will Be Delayed The New York Times South Sudan postpones first-ever national elections until February Al Jazeera Was it lawful to delay South Sudan’s elections until February 2027? Radio Tamazuj
articles.content: JUBA, South Sudan (AP) — South Sudan has again postponed its first national elections since independence in 2011, moving polling from December to February amid concerns about insecurity, funding shortages and the country’s readiness to vote. A revised timetable published Saturday by the National Election Commission sets Feb. 11, 2027, as polling day, replacing Dec. 22. The document did not give a reason for the postponement. The polls have been repeatedly delayed, including in 2022 and 2024. The latest announcement follows warnings that elections could further unravel the country’s fragile peace. The commission published the timetable on social media on the day voter registration was scheduled to begin. It also sets dates for candidate nominations and campaigning. A day earlier, commission chairperson Gabriel Bol Deng told journalists in Juba that registration would run from Nov. 14 to Nov. 28 at 3,161 registration centers across the country’s 10 states and three administrative areas. Deng urged eligible citizens to register and called on political parties, civil society groups, community leaders and the media to help raise public awareness. South Sudan became independent from Sudan in 2011 after decades of civil war. A new conflict broke out in 2013 between forces loyal to President Salva Kiir and followers of his rival, Riek Machar. A peace deal was signed in 2018 and a transitional government of national unity was formed in 2020. Fighting between government and opposition forces escalated in early 2025, and Machar was placed under house arrest in Juba that March. He and seven co-defendants are on trial on charges including treason, murder and crimes against humanity linked to an attack on an army garrison in Nasir, in the northeast. They deny the charges. The transitional unity government was dissolved in September and replaced by a caretaker administration. The South Sudan Civil Society Forum said in a statement issued in late October that conditions did not support fair, credible, peaceful and inclusive elections within the remaining time. It called for an inclusive dialogue on electoral preparations and the country’s transition. Kiir’s ruling Sudan People’s Liberation Movement, or SPLM, has been holding primaries across the country. But there has been little electoral activity among other registered parties, Anita Kiki Gbeho, head of the United Nations Mission in South Sudan, told the U.N. Security Council on Nov. 10. “Elections must be a milestone in the transition, not its conclusion. Elections cannot substitute for political dialogue, confidence-building and continued implementation of the Peace Agreement,” she said. On Thursday, two SPLM delegates were killed in an attack in Miri Loko village, in Western Equatoria state, while returning from party primaries and congresses, officials said. It was the third security incident affecting the party’s primaries and congresses in the state, according to Deng Dau Deng, who chairs the SPLM’s high-level committee there. One of those killed was Veronica Lucy Gordon, a former South Sudan Broadcasting Corporation journalist who had recently been nominated to contest a women’s seat in the National Legislative Assembly. Edmund Yakani, director of the Community Empowerment for Progress Organization, condemned the attack, urging those opposed to the delegates’ political views to pursue dialogue rather than violence. Following news of the postponement, Yakani called for transparency in the commission’s decisions. He also said the locations of registration centers remained unpublished on the day registration was scheduled to begin, leaving citizens without clear information about where to register.

Dubious buys raise alarm over local control of opioid cash
articles.description: State and local governments spent about $3.7 billion in opioid settlement funds last year. That’s more than the median annual income of 42,000 American families combined. The money comes from companies that were sued for aggressively pushing painkillers and fueling the opioid crisis. Large amounts went to addiction treatment, recovery housing, and other initiatives that […]
articles.content: Dalton Barrett is a paramedic in Edgecombe County, North Carolina, where he leads the post-overdose response team and oversees the county’s opioid settlement funds. He says opioid money should support interventions that help people move from addiction toward recovery, not medical equipment that should be covered by the general budget. “People that suffer from addiction are looking for trust,” he says. “They’re not looking for fancy equipment.” (Boogielou Johnson)State and local governments spent about $3.7 billion in opioid settlement funds last year. That’s more than the median annual income of 42,000 American families combined. The money comes from companies that were sued for aggressively pushing painkillers and fueling the opioid crisis. Large amounts went to addiction treatment, recovery housing, and other initiatives that many public health researchers and families affected by the crisis agree fit the spirit of the settlements — to save lives and remediate the problem. But other expenditures had tenuous ties to addiction, including: $150,000 for street lighting in Camden, New Jersey. $130,000 for Flock cameras in Carmel, Indiana. At least $84,000 for city insurance, building utilities, vehicle repairs, and other standard city expenses in Mullens, West Virginia. $36,200 for a pickleball court in Gilmer County, West Virginia. KFF Health News uncovered these expenditures among about 17,500 examined through a yearlong investigation with the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and Shatterproof, a national nonprofit focused on addiction. The team filed public records requests, scoured government websites, and extracted expenditures, which were then sorted into categories such as treatment or prevention. The result is the most comprehensive national database documenting how opioid settlement money was used (or left unspent) in 2025. The pot of settlement cash, which many addiction survivors and their advocates consider “blood money,” is expected to total about $60 billion over nearly two decades. It is split among state governments, counties, cities, and specially created opioid settlement councils in some places. Although there are some spending guidelines within the settlement agreements, there is considerable flexibility, a vacuum of leadership and oversight, and significant gaps in how the public can track the dollars. Much of the questionable spending — ranging from law enforcement gadgets to mundane municipal needs — happens at the county and city level, where local leaders often have no background in addiction policy and sometimes award the money to the first people who ask for it. Nationwide, local decision-makers control nearly half the money, according to OpioidSettlementTracker.com, a site dedicated to following this cash. Proponents of local control say these officials know their communities best and are closest to the problem. But as dubious expenditures mount, some recovery advocates question if county and city officials are equipped to handle this once-in-a-generation opportunity. “It shouldn’t be run by these politicians,” said Elizabeth Burke Beaty, a person in recovery and a New Jersey-based advocate who’s been following the opioid cash for years. Elizabeth Burke Beaty is executive director of the Sea Change Recovery Community and Harm Reduction Center in Ocean County, New Jersey. She says people directly affected by the addiction crisis understand gaps in their local community care systems best and should be the ones deciding how to spend opioid cash. “This whole opioid settlement should be run by the people who’ve lost everything,” she says. (Elizabeth Burke Beaty) She said people directly affected by the crisis understand gaps in their local community care systems best and have the most insight into how funds can be used effectively. “This whole opioid settlement should be run by the people who’ve lost everything,” she said. As executive director of the Sea Change Recovery Community and Harm Reduction Center in Ocean County, Burke Beaty sees those people daily. A woman who lost her brother and father to addiction and later landed in the hospital herself. An 11-year-old boy, holding his grandfather’s hand at an overdose awareness event, as they mourned a family member. “This is money from dead people and people left behind,” Burke Beaty said. Of course, many local officials have lost friends and family to the crisis as well, and many care deeply about putting the money to good use. Unlike state officials, who have access to health departments with specific expertise and staff whose entire job is writing policy, local decision-makers often work with bare-bones support. They may juggle other jobs alongside their official duties and can be bombarded by aggressive sales tactics from companies that view the settlements as a gold rush. They must determine how to make an impact with opioid settlement cash while facing the sober reality of needing to balance a government budget, keep public schools running, and ensure roads are maintained. Burke Beaty acknowledges these challenges and offers to work with many local leaders in her area, often writing letters, showing up at public meetings, and creating reports with detailed feedback on how localities spent the money. But when these efforts go ignored, she wonders if it’s because of a lack of resources or “a lack of willingness to do the right thing,” she said. “Did this come from a place of ignorance or an ‘I don’t care’ place?” Who Should Control the Money? It can be tempting to suggest state governments should oversee all the cash, especially as some debatable spending patterns emerge at the local level. But that’s been tried before. In the Tobacco Master Settlement of 1998, cigarette companies paid hundreds of billions of dollars to states, typically without county or city involvement. Ultimately, much of the money went to plugging budget gaps, and, over 20 years, less than 3% of tobacco settlement and tax-related revenue was directed to anti-smoking programs. “It is not likely that whatever model we pick is going to work flawlessly,” said Philip Rutherford, who leads substance use strategy at the National Council for Mental Wellbeing, a nonprofit representing community mental health and addiction treatment organizations. Splitting the opioid money with local governments offers some advantages, he added. They spend less on administrative costs, can pivot more quickly as the drug landscape changes, and can test innovations. It’s also not unusual for local officials to involve themselves in areas in which they lack personal expertise, said Annie Qing, who oversees health and human services work at the National Association of Counties. “There are a lot of county commissioners that are making decisions on roads that may not be construction experts,” Qing said. Their role is to seek out subject matter experts, combine their knowledge with what they know their community needs, and identify investments “that make the most sense for their county.” For support in allocating opioid settlement cash, they can turn to universities, county associations, and national public health and policy groups. Saving Lives — But From Overdose or Cardiac Arrest? Still, it can be tricky to apply academic research and high-level principles to the messy, on-the-ground realities of settlement spending. Take the case of automated external defibrillators, or AEDs. These portable electronic devices can save lives in the event of sudden cardiac arrest. Last year, about 100 localities across 20 states committed $3.7 million in opioid funds to expenditures that included AEDs, cardiac monitors, and related accessories. Many local leaders saw the purchases as saving lives from overdose, though the science doesn’t quite back them up. Southfield, Michigan, purchased six Lifepak cardiac monitors and related supplies for about $350,000. Mayor Kenson Siver said overdose response has become increasingly complex, as people often use a mix of opioids and stimulants, and that paramedics need to be prepared for a range of situations. Cardiac monitors go beyond traditional AEDs to measure how effectively someone is breathing, he said, which can help emergency responders determine if “interventions are working and identify deterioration or complications that require additional treatment.” However, emergency medical responders say there’s a fundamental misunderstanding. AEDs and cardiac monitors are critical public health tools — but they are rarely used for opioid overdoses. “I’m not saying that you never will, but the number is so low,” said Dalton Barrett, a paramedic in Edgecombe County, North Carolina, where he leads the post-overdose response team and oversees the county’s opioid settlement funds. In opioid overdoses, people stop breathing. They typically need oxygen or naloxone, a medication that can reverse overdoses. AEDs work only in cardiac emergencies and when the machine can detect a shockable heart rhythm — not common among overdose victims, Barrett said. When jurisdictions buy AEDs with opioid dollars, they’re more likely plugging gaps in their general budget, which should be covering required ambulance equipment, he said. “I have a hard time identifying this as a particularly strong or targeted use of settlement funds.” The only exception would be if a jurisdiction started a new ambulance team dedicated to overdose response and needed an AED to bring the vehicle to code, he said. Generally, Barrett would prefer that opioid cash be spent hiring someone to follow up with people who have overdosed and connect them to treatment, housing, or other resources. “People that suffer from addiction are looking for trust,” he said. “They’re not looking for fancy equipment.” Dalton Barrett is a paramedic in Edgecombe County, North Carolina, where he leads the post-overdose response team and oversees the county’s opioid settlement funds. He says opioid money should support interventions that help people move from addiction toward recovery, not medical equipment that should be covered by the general budget. “People that suffer from addiction are looking for trust,” he says. “They’re not looking for fancy equipment.” (Boogielou Johnson) A Lack of Teeth Some advocates are calling on states to rein in local governments’ spending from the settlements. But no one is eager to take on that role. State officials don’t win friends by exerting control over local money. And, in some cases, they’re barred from doing so. Jennifer Tourville is executive director of a University of Tennessee initiative that provides guidance to local governments on spending opioid cash. Her team’s work is funded by the state’s opioid abatement council. “We aren’t permitted to tell counties what they can and cannot buy,” she said. “We try and provide guidance on the intent of the funds and what would be most impactful for their community.” A few states have issued lists of items that opioid money cannot be used for, often called unallowable lists. They generally include law enforcement tools, such as body cameras and drones, as well as general emergency medical supplies, such as first aid kits and gloves. But even those lists sometimes lack teeth. For instance, Spencer County, Indiana, spent about $16,700 on eight new AEDs for its sheriff department — even though AEDs appeared on Indiana’s unallowable list, as they do on three other states’. When asked if there’d be repercussions for the county, the Indiana Commission to Combat Substance Use Disorder said the unallowable list was simply guidance. “Statute does not grant the state any enforcement authority related to how local entities spend opioid settlement funds,” said Shelby Thomas, a spokesperson for the commission. Spencer County leaders did not respond to requests for comment. A similar situation occurred in Iowa.
